title: No Twin Letters Side by Side
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Rearrange its letters so that no two neighbouring characters are the same, and return the new string. It must use exactly the letters of s, each as many times as it appears.

If no such arrangement exists, return the empty string "". When several arrangements work, any of them is accepted.

examples.why: Three a's need two other letters between them, and b and c are exactly enough. "acaba" would also be accepted.
Three a's need at least two separators, and there is only one other letter.
Pairing letters off greedily as "aabb..." fails; spreading them works. Any valid order is fine.

hints: When is it impossible? Think about the most common letter and how many other letters you need to separate its copies.
Build the answer left to right. At each step, which letter is the safest to place next?
Use a max-heap of (count, letter). Take the most frequent letter that differs from the one you just placed, place it, and push it back with one less count.

explain.intuition:
The most frequent letter is the only real danger. With k copies of it you need at least k − 1 other letters as separators, so an answer exists exactly when maxCount ≤ ceil(n / 2).

A greedy that always places the letter with the most copies left (but not the same as the last one placed) never paints itself into a corner: it keeps the remaining counts as even as possible, so the dangerous letter keeps getting spent. A max-heap gives that letter in O(log 26). Hold back the letter you just used for one step, then return it to the heap. Like a scheduler with a cooldown of one slot.
steps: Count each letter. If any count is greater than (n + 1) / 2 (rounded down), return "".
Put every (count, letter) in a max-heap.
Pop the top letter and append it. If a letter was held back from the previous step and still has copies, push it back now.
Hold back the letter just used, with its count reduced by one. Repeat until the heap is empty.
pitfalls: Pushing the letter you just used straight back into the heap. It can come out on top again and land next to itself.
Checking impossibility with maxCount > n / 2. For odd n, "aba" has 2 a's out of 3 and is fine; the limit is ceil(n / 2).
Sorting once by frequency and writing letters in that order. "aabbcc" would come out as "aabbcc".

complexity.time: O(n log k), k ≤ 26 distinct letters

solutions.title: Max-heap, hold back the last letter
solutions.idea: Always place the letter with the most copies left, skipping the one just placed by keeping it out of the heap for one step.

solutions.title: Fill even slots, then odd slots
solutions.idea: Write the most frequent letter into positions 0, 2, 4, … first, then continue with the other letters, wrapping to positions 1, 3, 5, … when the even slots run out.

followups: Same letters must now be at least k positions apart, not just 1. How does the hold-back step change?
Return the alphabetically smallest valid arrangement instead of any one.
